segments.say: On the bus home this evening, Hana wasn't reading. She was staring out of the window at the wet streets. And yet, she was far from idle. In the space of twenty minutes, her mind replayed a moment from the meeting, imagined a conversation with her sister that hasn't happened yet, pictured what she might cook on Sunday, and wandered, for no clear reason, back to a beach she knew as a child. Four little stories, none of which she chose to tell.

Psychologists call this mind wandering. It's when our attention drifts away from what's in front of us, toward thoughts about the past, the future, other people, or things that might happen. And very often, those thoughts take the form of stories. Little scenes, with people in them, wanting things, saying things, and things happening next.

How often does this happen? In 2010, Matthew Killingsworth and Daniel Gilbert, at Harvard University, used a smartphone app to find out. At random moments during the day, it asked 2,250 adults three questions. What are you doing right now? Are you thinking about something other than what you're doing? And how are you feeling?

show.what: An iPhone app asked 2,250 adults at random moments what they were doing, whether they were thinking about something else, and how happy they felt. Minds were wandering in nearly half of the samples.

segments.say: The answer was striking. In about forty-seven percent of the moments sampled, people were thinking about something other than what they were doing. Nearly half of waking life, it seemed, was spent somewhere else, in the stories of the mind.

show.title: Killingsworth & Gilbert, 2010
show.label: of the moments sampled, people's minds were wandering from what they were doing

segments.say: The study also found that, on average, people reported feeling a little less happy when their minds were wandering than when they weren't. That held even when they wandered to pleasant topics, which didn't make them happier than staying with what they were doing. The researchers suggested, in their title, that a wandering mind is an unhappy mind.

It's worth being careful with that conclusion. It's an average across many people and moments, and wandering minds aren't always unhappy ones. Other researchers have found that it depends a lot on what the mind wanders to, and on whether we let it wander on purpose. A pleasant daydream on a quiet afternoon is a very different thing from going over a worry again and again.

Around the same time, brain researchers were noticing something interesting. When people lie quietly in a scanner, not doing any particular task, a set of brain areas becomes more active rather than less. It's been called the default mode network. And in 2007, a team led by Malia Mason published a study in Science linking this network to mind wandering.

They had people practice simple tasks until they became very familiar, then did brain scans while those people performed both the practiced tasks and new ones. With the familiar tasks, people reported more mind wandering. And the default network was more active, especially in people who said their minds tended to wander more in daily life.

show.what: People practiced simple tasks until they became easy, then did them in a brain scanner. Easy, practiced tasks left more room for mind wandering, and the default network was more active when the mind wandered more.

segments.say: Many studies have linked this network to some very story-like kinds of thinking. Remembering our own past. Imagining our future. Thinking about what other people are thinking. In other words, when the brain isn't busy with the world in front of it, one of the things it seems to do is tell itself stories, about us and the people in our lives.

In a way, it's the interpreter from earlier, and the narrative identity, working quietly in the background. Rehearsing, replaying, imagining. Keeping our story going, even when we're just looking out of a bus window at the rain.

And mind wandering isn't only a distraction. In 2012, a team led by Benjamin Baird asked people to think of as many unusual uses as they could for ordinary objects, like a brick. Then they took a short break. Some did a demanding task, some an easy one that let their minds wander, some rested, and some had no break. Afterward, they returned to the same problems.

show.where: University of California, Santa Barbara, USA
show.what: People worked on a creative problem, then took a break doing an easy task, a hard task, or resting. After the easy task, which allowed the most mind wandering, people improved most on the problems they had seen before.

segments.say: The people who had done the easy, mind-wandering task improved the most on the problems they'd already seen. The researchers suggested that letting the mind wander during a break might give ideas a chance to recombine, quietly, in the background. Many people know this feeling. The answer that arrives in the shower, or on a walk, once you've stopped trying.

So here's what we've learned about the storyteller inside. Our minds wander for a large part of the day. On average, wandering goes with feeling a little less happy, though it depends on where it goes. A network of brain areas seems to support it, and it's linked to remembering, imagining and thinking about others. And sometimes, letting the mind wander helps new ideas take shape.

show.title: Stories in your head
items: Minds wander about half the time
Wandering often feels a bit less happy

segments.say: And at night, in bed, with no screen and no task, the inner storyteller can become louder. That's when the replays and rehearsals often arrive. Many people find that a gentle story, read or heard at bedtime, helps them settle. It gives the storyteller something soft to follow, instead of the day's worries.

So we tell stories about triangles, about ghosts, about Linda, about our days, our whole lives, and endlessly, quietly, to ourselves. And there's one more place to visit before we rest, the oldest storytelling place of all. Because researchers have spent nights with people living in very traditional ways, listening to what they talk about after dark. And what they found says something about why stories and nighttime seem to belong together.
